---
title: "Robustness at Scale: How fragile are empirical economic results?"
---
**Speaker:** Johanna Einsiedler, University of Basel

**Co-authors:** Elizabeth Rhodes (Open Research), Francis DiTraglia (University of Oxford)

### Abstract {.unlisted .unnumbered}

How much, and when, should we trust published scientific findings? Recent large-scale replication efforts across economics, psychology, and the biomedical sciences have produced a mixed picture: some findings hold up well under independent re-examination, while others fail to replicate or shrink substantially in re-estimation. These efforts have focused attention on whether results survive new data, new samples, or independent re-analysis.

A complementary and underexplored question is how sensitive a published finding is to its own data. If the original sample had been just slightly different — for example a handful of observations missing, mis-recorded, or excluded for principled reasons — would the headline conclusion still stand? Broderick, Giordano, and Meager (2023) recently formalized this question with the Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP), a fast method for identifying the smallest fraction of observations whose removal would flip the sign of an estimate, its statistical significance, or both. Applied to a handful of well-known studies, AMIP revealed striking fragility: in several cases, dropping less than 1% of the sample was enough to overturn the headline result.

We apply this diagnostic at scale to empirical papers from top Economics journals, published over the last ten years. For each paper, an automated pipeline downloads the replication package, identifies all headline specifications and computes AMIP for sign, significance, and joint changes. For the subset of studies covered by the Experimental Economics Replication Project (Camerer et al., 2016), we additionally ask whether AMIP-based sensitivity predicts whether the original finding successfully replicated.

Preliminary findings indicate that many high-profile published results are highly sensitive to small data perturbations: in some specifications, dropping even a single observation is enough to change the qualitative conclusion. Beyond what this implies for empirical economics, the project speaks to broader metascientific questions about how robustness diagnostics should be developed, evaluated, and reported across methodological disciplines.
